## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Seyyajātaka* (Ja 282) is a canonical story in the Pali *Jātaka* collection. The narrative opening relates that the Buddha delivered the tale while residing at Jetavana in reference to a courtier of the king of Kosala [Fausböll 1879]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was born as a king of Benares (Bārāṇasī) who chose nonviolence, refusing to wage war to protect his kingdom because doing so would inflict injury and suffering [Jerryson and Juergensmeyer 2010; Fausböll 1879]. When captured and cast into prison by an invading rival, the Bodhisatta felt intense compassion toward his conqueror for the painful karmic retributions the latter would incur [Jerryson and Juergensmeyer 2010]. Through the force of this compassion, the invading king was afflicted with severe bodily torment until he repented, liberated the Bodhisatta, and restored the kingdom [Jerryson and Juergensmeyer 2010]. In the concluding identification (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identified the invading king as Ānanda and the virtuous king of Benares as himself [Fausböll 1879]. The verse text opens with the phrase *Seyyaso seyyaso hoti* [Fausböll 1879].
